Technical Report
November 2026

 

Lara Mini Base

Language diversity as a resource, not a trade-off

Translated, Lara Team

Contents

Abstract

General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architectures reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.

1  Introduction

Small base language models have improved mostly by reading ever more tokens, and recent models with only a few billion parameters are trained on more than ten trillion of them (Yang et al., 2025a; Hugging Face, 2025c). Because high-quality English text is limited, a growing budget also ends up repeating the same data, with diminishing returns (Muennighoff et al., 2025a). Rather than reading the same English text again and again, we suggest that a small model should spend part of its budget on the text it has seen least: text in other languages.

Text in other languages may offer more than new tokens. Research on multi-task learning has shown that related tasks can improve generalization by sharing learned representations (Caruana, 1997). Similarly, multilingual neural machine translation has demonstrated positive transfer between languages (Firat et al., 2016). More broadly, representation learning suggests that different observations can help a model discover shared explanatory factors underlying the data (Bengio et al., 2013). These findings motivate a hypothesis: different languages may provide complementary perspectives on the same underlying reality, helping a shared model learn more generalizable representations. Such benefits could potentially extend beyond multilingual tasks to English reasoning and other capabilities.

Even counting second-language speakers, English has only about 1.5 billion speakers: most of the world’s population does not speak it (Eberhard et al., 2025). Text in these languages is also widely available in open corpora (Nguyen et al., 2024; Penedo et al., 2025; Oepen et al., 2026). Yet the general-purpose open base models that disclose their mixture contribute at most 12% of their tokens to this text (Table 1). Models built for European languages give it 21% to 51%, but in our evaluation they score far below general-purpose models of the same size. For example, EuroLLM-1.7B and Apertus-v1.1-1.5B reach an average benchmark score of 27.6 and 31.2, against 53.8 for Qwen3-1.7B (Table 18). At first glance, these scores suggest that multilingual data cost a small model its general ability.

This leaves an open question: can a model with a small active-parameter budget be strong across many languages without sacrificing its English? Earlier work found that languages compete for the capacity of a small model, so adding languages can hurt each language (Conneau et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024). Recent scaling laws show that this trade-off depends on the size of the model and on how data are allocated across languages (Longpre et al., 2026). The answer, therefore, depends not only on how much multilingual data a model is trained on but also on how it is chosen and used.

We address this question with Lara Mini base, a multilingual mixture of experts base model with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters, pretrained from scratch on 6T tokens. We built Lara Mini base around its data. From openly released datasets, we assembled a deduplicated and filtered pool in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. The first three training stages (main, transition and anneal) read 6T tokens from this pool and move toward high-quality, question-answer, code and math data. English makes up only 41% of the 6T tokens. English falls from 44% of the main stage to 27% of the anneal, so that the other languages grow from 46% to 55% of the text and outweigh English in the anneal (Section 2). Of the 6T training tokens, 97% are the first read of a document (Section 2.3). A fourth and last stage of 100B tokens then extends the context of Lara Mini base to 128k tokens (Section 4.1). To support many languages while keeping inference cost low, every layer of Lara Mini base has a fine-grained mixture of experts that activates 4 of 128 experts per token. To keep the inference state small, the layers interleave Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025c), sliding-window and global attention, the latter in only 7 of the 34 layers (Section 3).

We compare Lara Mini base with 56 open base models on standard English, multilingual, math and code benchmarks, all evaluated by us with the same harness and settings. As in Muennighoff et al. (2025b), we group the models by active parameters, as a rough approximation of inference cost (Section 5.1). Among the 36 models with up to 2B active parameters, Lara Mini base ranks first on the average of the four domains, with 57.0, 3.1 points above the next model (Figure 1). It also ranks first on the multilingual average in the languages it supports, 3.4 points ahead. It leads even though this group includes models with more than 3 times its active parameters. The next two models, granite-4.0-h-tiny and Qwen3-1.7B, were trained on 22.5T and 36T tokens, about 4 and 6 times as many (Table 6). Lara Mini base also outscores several models with 6 to 13 times its active parameters, such as Ministral-3-3B (53.8), Gemma-4-E4B (55.4) and Llama-3.1-8B (51.2). Among the models we evaluated from European developers, it is the strongest, ahead of Apertus-v1.5-8B (55.8) and Domyn-Edge (55.4). Although English accounts for less than half of its training data, Lara Mini base ranks second in its group for English. When the multilingual third of the anneal is replaced with English, the English average rises by only 0.3 points and the multilingual average falls by 2.7 (Section 6.1). An expert routing analysis reveals that experts are shared across languages, which is consistent with this ablation hardly deteriorating performance on English tasks (Section 6.2).

These results come at a small inference cost. Lara Mini base needs the compute per token of a small dense model, although all its parameters must be held in memory. For a single user on one A100 GPU, without quantization, it generates about 1,100 characters per second (Figure 5). This speed matches that of dense models with about 1B parameters and is at least 1.8 times that of every model that scores higher on average.

We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license11 1 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/, which allows research and other non-commercial use. We will also release T-HellaSwag, a machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) into 110 language variants, of higher quality than the commonly used Multilingual HellaSwag (Lai et al., 2023) (Appendix F).

Section 2 describes the pretraining data, Section 3 the architecture and Section 4 training operations. Section 5 reports evaluation methods and results. Section 6 analyses the benefits of our data choices on multilingual and English tasks. The Appendix contains additional technical detail aimed at sharing our insights with the open LLM community.

2  Pretraining Data

Unlike general-purpose models, Lara Mini base is not trained mostly on English: English accounts for only 41% of its 6T training tokens.22 2 The English domain of Table 2. Code, math and SFT-like data, mostly in English, are counted as separate domains. The 44 other languages account for at least three times the share of general-purpose open base models that disclose them (Table 1). In absolute terms, Lara Mini base processes more multilingual tokens than Llama 3, SmolLM3, or Nemotron Nano 2, even though they train on 11.2T to 20T tokens. Its share is within the range of the models for European languages in Table 1, all of which have at least 1.7B active parameters, against 0.6B for Lara Mini base. Smaller multilingual models exist, such as EuroMoE-2.6B-A0.6B and Apertus-v1.1-0.5B, but score far below Lara Mini base (Table 18).

All data come from openly released datasets (Tables 2 and 2.1), which Translated’s internal pipeline deduplicates and filters into a training pool of 13.8T tokens (Section 2.2). We sample 6T tokens from this pool in three stages (main, transition and anneal), moving toward high-quality data (Figure 2). Explicit rules set the mixture of each stage (Tables 3 and 2.3). A fourth stage of 100B tokens then extends the context from 4,096 to 128k tokens (Section 2.3).

2.1  Data Sources

Besides web, PDF and Wikipedia text (Table 2), 26% of the training tokens (1.58T) are synthetic, most of them from NVIDIA’s Nemotron collections. The largest part is English web text rewritten by language models; the rest is code, math, SFT-like data (examples in the format of supervised fine-tuning data) and multilingual question-answer data. The multilingual question-answer data make up 13% of the multilingual tokens and are mostly machine-translated from English into 16 of our languages. Appendix A lists every data group with its sources and licenses (Table 9) and shows how deduplication and selection reduce the collected data to the pool (Figure 8).

2.2  Deduplication and Filtering

We remove exact copies over the whole pool at once, so that a text kept from one source is removed from every other. We then remove near-duplicates with the MinHash (Broder, 1997; Lee et al., 2022) implementation of Marin (Marin Community, 2025), within each language across all its sources, and within code. Synthetic and rewritten data are not compared for near-duplicates with the pages they rephrase. Deduplication keeps about 30T of the 50T collected tokens. Most duplicates occur across sources, so per-source deduplication would miss them: FineWeb-Edu, for instance, keeps only 15% of its tokens after deduplication against the other sources.

For quality, we use the model-based quality signals released with the main corpora. In English web data, high quality means the two highest classes of Nemotron-CC and FineWeb-Edu. The medium class of Nemotron-CC is used only before the anneal. In multilingual web data, high quality means FineWeb2-HQ, the pages that a model-based filter ranks highest in each language. Math is split in the same way by the quality tiers of its sources. On top of these signals, Translated’s internal pipeline applies further filters of its own, built on the company’s experience with multilingual data.

The selected data, tokenized with the Qwen3 tokenizer, form the training pool (Table 10). Besides all the high-quality data, the pool holds more plain web text (web data below the high-quality level) than training needs. Training reads only about a fifth of this plain web text.

Decontamination.

We scanned the whole training pool for the items of our evaluation benchmarks. The scan follows Brown et al. (2020): it matches long word n-grams (character n-grams in scripts written without spaces) and flags the documents that share a large part of a benchmark item. Flagged documents make up about 0.03% of the pool’s tokens. Benchmarks whose items circulate widely on the web, mostly in English, math and code, are the most exposed, while the benchmarks of our multilingual domain are much less so. Of the first three stages, only the anneal is decontaminated, as in Kolibri (Aleph Alpha, 2026): it skips training sequences that contain a flagged document without changing the mixture. The tests in Section D.4 show no evidence that Lara Mini base memorized the contaminated items: its scores are consistent with generalization and not inflated by contamination.

2.3  Data Mixture and Curriculum

We designed the mixture to achieve competence in 44 languages besides English, with priority given to the official EU languages. It also had to keep English knowledge and reasoning on par with English-centric models of the same size, while adding basic code and math abilities. We set it with explicit rules rather than by optimizing mixture weights on proxy models. Each rule rests on published evidence, data availability, or our priorities among languages (Table 3). Figure 2 shows the resulting mixture of each stage.

Of the four stages of pretraining, the first three read 6T tokens in 4,096-token sequences. The main stage, 4.8T tokens at constant learning rate, uses the broadest mixture. The transition stage, with 0.6T tokens still at a constant learning rate, moves the mixture halfway toward the anneal mixture. The anneal of the last 0.6T tokens decays the learning rate to zero. As in earlier work, the learning rate decays only at the end (Hu et al., 2024; Hägele et al., 2024) and training ends on high-quality data (Feng et al., 2024). A sudden change in data can cause a model to forget what it learned earlier, and keeping part of the earlier mixture reduces this forgetting (Ibrahim et al., 2024). The transition stage therefore splits the change into two smaller steps, as the two-blend schedule of Parmar et al. (2024) does in continued pretraining. Over the three stages, code, math and SFT-like data grow from 19% to 40% of the tokens, and the anneal keeps only high-quality English web data. The multilingual share stays at about a third while English falls from 44% to 27%, so that in the anneal multilingual text is the largest domain, ahead of English (Figure 2). Of the text in English and the other languages, without code, math and SFT-like data, the other languages make up 46% in the main stage, 50% in the transition and 55% in the anneal. Its content also shifts toward high-quality sources: plain web text falls from 41% of the multilingual tokens to 6.5%, while high-quality web and question-answer data rise from 39% to 69%.

We include every language with at least 20B tokens after deduplication. Irish and Maltese have far fewer speakers, but we include them so that all 24 official languages of the European Union are covered. This gives 44 languages besides English (Table 11). Sampling languages by size would give Russian and Chinese a third of the multilingual tokens. Flatter sampling trades quality in high-resource languages for quality in low-resource ones (Conneau et al., 2020). We therefore sample languages more evenly than by size, with extra weight given to the official EU languages and to a selection of widely spoken languages outside the EU. Compared with size-based sampling, these weights raise the share of official EU languages from 46% to 61% of multilingual tokens, mostly at the expense of Russian, Chinese and Japanese (Figure 9).

Because mixtures of experts are sensitive to repeated data (Jha et al., 2026), we cap the epochs of each source within the 6T budget, as in UniMax (Chung et al., 2023). No source is read more than twice except Wikipedia, and plain web text is repeated only in Irish and Maltese. In all, 97% of the training tokens are the first read of a document (Table 10).

Long-context stage.

The fourth stage reads 100B tokens in two steps: 40B in 32k-token sequences, then 60B in 128k-token sequences (Section 4.1). As in Kolibri (Aleph Alpha, 2026), both steps mix the anneal mixture as is, the same mixture reweighted toward long documents, and natural long documents from FinePDFs (Hugging Face, 2025a) and, in the 32k step only, FineWeb2-HQ (Messmer et al., 2025) (Table 12). Both steps also give about 11% of their tokens to math and code: Nemotron-CC-Math documents of up to 16k tokens (Karimi Mahabadi et al., 2026), real (not synthetic) code and, in the 32k step only, SFT-like math documents of 16k to 32k tokens (Table 9). Keeping the anneal mixture limits the loss of short-context quality (Gao et al., 2025; Team Olmo, 2025). It therefore makes up half of the 128k step, which ends training. Across the whole stage, 58% of tokens come from documents longer than 4k tokens, and 12.3B tokens come from documents of at least 128k tokens.

3  Architecture

The architecture of Lara Mini base follows two goals: capacity for many languages at a small active budget, and a small inference state. The mixture of experts (MoE) layers serve the first: in our small-scale comparisons, a fine-grained MoE outperformed dense models with more than twice its active parameters (Section C.1). The hybrid token mixing serves the second. Only 7 of the 34 layers use global attention, so the memory held per sequence grows with context length about five times more slowly than in a full-attention model of the same shape.

Lara Mini base is a decoder-only Transformer with an MoE feed-forward block in every layer and three kinds of token mixer: Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025c), sliding-window attention and global attention. It has 7.2B parameters in total, of which 0.6B are active for each token (Table 4). The routed experts hold 94% of all parameters (6.8B). Of the active parameters, 24% are the tied input and output embedding, 41% the four routed experts and the shared expert that each token passes through, and 35% the token mixers, routers and normalization weights. The remaining building blocks are standard: pre-normalization with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), SwiGLU feed-forward networks (Shazeer, 2020) and no bias terms. The model uses the Qwen3 tokenizer (Yang et al., 2025a), with a vocabulary of 151,669 tokens (151,936 rows in the embedding table, padded). Figure 3 shows one layer and the order of the token mixers.

3.1  Hybrid Token Mixing

A Transformer with global attention in every layer caches the keys and values of all previous tokens. Its memory per sequence therefore grows linearly with context length and dominates the cost of serving long contexts. Lara Mini base instead interleaves three token mixers with complementary strengths, in short blocks, each ending with a global layer (Figure 3). A sliding-window layer is exact but sees only the last 512 tokens. A Gated DeltaNet layer captures the full context via a compressed state but struggles with precise local comparisons (Arora et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). Earlier hybrids therefore pair recurrent layers with local attention (De et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025). The global layers enable exact retrieval at any distance, whereas the other two’s memory does not grow with context. Gated DeltaNet can also make training more efficient: hybrids that use it in most layers match the quality of Transformers with substantially fewer training tokens (Merrill et al., 2026).

Gated DeltaNet.

Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025c) is a linear-attention layer whose state is a fixed-size matrix per head, updated with the gated delta rule:

𝐒t=αt​𝐒t−1​(𝐈−βt​𝐤t​𝐤t⊤)+βt​𝐯t​𝐤t⊤,𝐨t=𝐒t​𝐪t.\mathbf{S}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\,\mathbf{S}_{t-1}\left(\mathbf{I}-\beta_{t}\,\mathbf{k}_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top}\right)+\beta_{t}\,\mathbf{v}_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{o}_{t}=\mathbf{S}_{t}\,\mathbf{q}_{t}. (1)

The decay αt∈(0,1)\alpha_{t}\in(0,1) and the write strength βt∈(0,1)\beta_{t}\in(0,1) depend on the input token and are computed per head. The decay lets a head forget, and the delta rule (Schlag et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024) overwrites the value stored under a key instead of adding to it. Queries, keys and values pass through a causal depthwise convolution of width 4 followed by SiLU, and queries and keys are then L2-normalized. The output of each head is normalized with RMSNorm and gated with SiLU. The layer has no positional encoding: the recurrence itself carries the order of the tokens.

Sliding-window attention.

Sliding-window attention (Beltagy et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2023) restricts the attention of each token to the 512 most recent tokens, including itself. These layers use rotary position embeddings with base 10,000 over the full head dimension.

Global attention.

The global layers attend over the whole context and use no positional encoding (Kazemnejad et al., 2023), since the Gated DeltaNet and sliding-window layers below them already encode position. All attention layers, windowed and global, use grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) with 16 query and 4 key-value heads of dimension 128, and QK-norm.

Quality and memory.

We compared the token mixers in ablations at 100B tokens against a baseline with global attention in every layer (Section C.2). The hybrid achieved a lower held-out loss than the baseline, very close to that of a variant with Gated DeltaNet in all 26 non-global layers, whereas sliding windows alone did not lower it. The hybrid also had the largest mean benchmark gain over the baseline, matching an oracle that, for each benchmark, selects the better of the Gated DeltaNet and sliding-window variants. After a context extension to 32k tokens, the hybrid was also the best variant on RULER and ONERULER at that length, 4 to 8 points above both single-mixer variants (Table 16). As computed from the architecture, the memory used per sequence during generation is 468 MiB at 32k tokens and 1.77 GiB at 128k tokens. A model of the same shape with global attention in every layer would hold 2.13 GiB and 8.50 GiB.

3.2  Mixture of Experts Layers

Every layer of Lara Mini base has an MoE block with 128 routed experts and 1 shared expert (Dai et al., 2024), all of which are SwiGLU networks with a hidden size of 512. A linear router computes one logit per routed expert, in fp32. Each token is routed to its top-4 experts by router logit, and their outputs are weighted by a softmax over these 4 logits. The shared expert processes every token and its output is added without a gate. Routing is dropless (Gale et al., 2023): no expert has a capacity limit, and no token is dropped. A load-balancing loss (Fedus et al., 2022) with coefficient 10−310^{-3} pushes the router toward an even distribution of expert use. The experts are fine-grained: their hidden size is half the model width, and a token activates 1/321/32 of the routed parameters. We chose the number of experts and this sparsity through ablations (Section C.1). Section 6.2 analyzes how the trained model shares its experts across languages.

4  Training

All four stages of pretraining use a hybrid optimizer: Muon for the weight matrices of the layers and AdamW for the other parameters (Section 4.1). In the first three stages (Section 2.3), the learning rate remains constant until the anneal, then decays to zero (Table 5). The fourth stage extends the context to 128k tokens with its own learning-rate schedule (Section 4.1).

4.1  Pretraining Recipe

Optimizer.

Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) updates the layer weight matrices, experts included, and AdamW the other parameters; all of them share one learning rate and one weight decay (Table 5, details in Appendix B). In our ablations, AdamW needed 1.5 to 1.9 times as many tokens as Muon to reach the same training loss (Section C.1).

Stability measures.

Large logits are a common source of instability in bf16 training. Lara Mini base bounds logits after each softmax. Besides the query and key normalization (Henry et al., 2020) and the fp32 router of Section 3, it adds an output z-loss with coefficient 10−410^{-4} (Chowdhery et al., 2023) and a router z-loss of 10−310^{-3} (Zoph et al., 2022).

Long-context stage.

The long-context stage uses 100B tokens (Section 2.3), with the settings of Table 12 (Appendix B) taking over the last anneal optimizer state. These 100B tokens are 1.7% of the tokens of the first three stages, in line with the 0.8% to 1.8% of Olmo 3, Kolibri, SmolLM3 and Apertus (Team Olmo, 2025; Aleph Alpha, 2026; Hugging Face, 2025c; Hernández-Cano et al., 2026). The learning rate warms up to 8×10−58\times 10^{-5}, a tenth of the peak of the first three stages, and decays to zero over the last 15B tokens. The position encoding is unchanged: the global attention layers use none (Yang et al., 2025b), and the sliding-window layers never attend beyond 512 tokens (Section 3.1). Unlike in the first three stages, documents packed into one sequence do not interact: attention is masked across documents and the Gated DeltaNet state restarts at each document. Llama 3 found this masking important in continued pretraining on very long sequences (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Section 5.7 evaluates the result.

4.2  Training Dynamics

Training was stable throughout: the loss never exceeded its median over the preceding 1,000 steps by more than 3%, and expert utilization remained nearly uniform (Appendix B). Because the training loss shifts with the data mixture at each stage boundary, we followed progress on a fixed held-out set and on the evaluation suite of Section 5 (Figure 4). During the main stage, the Overall average (the mean of the four domain averages) rose gradually from 41.1 at 1.5T tokens to 44.1 at 4.6 T tokens. The transition stage, which increases the share of code and math, mainly improved these two domains. The anneal, which decays the learning rate on the highest-quality mixture, improved every domain. From the last checkpoint before the anneal (5.2T tokens) to its end, the Overall average rose by 10.5 points and math by 22.6. English and multilingual scores improved together at every evaluated checkpoint, both in the main stage and in the anneal.

5  Evaluation

We compare Lara Mini base against 56 open base models across 26 benchmarks in four domains: English knowledge and reasoning, multilingual understanding, math and code. The comparison tests whether a model trained on only 41% English data remains competitive in English and leads in the other languages. We evaluate the released Lara Mini base, the checkpoint after the long-context stage (Section 4.1); Section 5.7 reports its long-context results.

5.1  Evaluation Setup

Lara Mini base is a base model, so we evaluate it as one, with few-shot or zero-shot prompts (Brown et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2025) and no chat template. We compare it only with other pretrained base models, never with instruction-tuned ones. We score every model ourselves, with the same prompts, settings and answer extraction, using lm-evaluation-harness (Biderman et al., 2024). Log-likelihood tasks run on the Hugging Face backend with log-softmax in fp32, and generative tasks on vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). The two backends agree within 0.6 points on the tasks we checked.

Table 17 in Appendix D lists the benchmarks and their settings. We call the languages of the training data of Lara Mini base its supported languages. As is common for models trained on a defined set of languages (Martins et al., 2025b; Ali et al., 2025; Gonzalez-Agirre et al., 2025), we evaluate on the supported ones. Section D.2 reports the results per language. One multilingual benchmark, T-HellaSwag, is our own translation of HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) (Section 5.2). Each domain average is the mean of its benchmarks, and the Overall average gives the four domains equal weight. Code is scored by executing the generated programs. HumanEval is not in the suite, because all of its items occur in the public datasets of our training pool (Section 2.2).

Baselines.

Following Muennighoff et al. (2025b), we group the 56 baselines by active parameters, which approximate the cost of inference. The three groups have up to 2B, from 2B to 4B and more than 4B active parameters. The boundary between the last two groups is at 5B, so that the 4B models, with up to 4.7B active parameters, fall in the second. Gemma-4-E2B and Gemma-4-E4B, whose 5.1B and 7.9B parameters include per-layer embeddings, are placed at their 2B and 4B effective sizes. We checked that this grouping compares models of similar inference cost by measuring the generation speed of 45 of them on one GPU (Appendix E). For a single user, every measured model in the two larger groups generates text 1.4 to 4.2 times more slowly than Lara Mini base. In its own group, 21 of the 28 other measured models are slower as well. Table 6 shows 27 of the 56 baselines, and Section D.1 reports all 56 models on every benchmark, including those named in the text but not in the table.

5.2  T-HellaSwag

T-HellaSwag is our higher-quality machine translation of the English commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) into 110 language variants of 105 languages; we include it in our evaluation suite and will release it. The variants are written in 25 scripts, and 46 of them use a script other than Latin. Each variant holds 200 documents, 22,000 in all, selected for translation quality while keeping the difficulty of the English originals. T-HellaSwag-full holds all 10,042 translated documents of each variant. A multilingual version of HellaSwag already exists, Multilingual HellaSwag (Lai et al., 2023), which covers 33 languages. We compared the two translations across 50 documents per language using two LLM judges: Gemini 4 Argon (Google DeepMind, 2026) and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026). In the 32 languages they share, both judges preferred our translation in more than 98% of the documents. Appendix F describes how we translated and selected the documents, how we assessed the translation quality, and the limitations of the dataset.

5.3  Main Results

Among the 36 models with up to 2B active parameters (Table 6), Lara Mini base ranks first overall (57.0, 3.1 points above granite-4.0-h-tiny) and on the multilingual average (56.7, 3.4 points above Gemma-4-E2B). It is also first on math, second on English and fifth on code. Six of the 56 models score higher overall and six on the multilingual average, all in the two larger groups, with 4 to 14 times as many active parameters as Lara Mini base (Table 18). Of these models, the four that report their pretraining tokens were trained on 18T to 36T, 3 to 6 times as many as Lara Mini base. Lara Mini base also scores higher overall than several models with 6 to 13 times its active parameters, such as Ministral-3-3B, Gemma-4-E4B, Apertus-v1.5-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Figure 1 summarizes the same results.

Efficiency.

Figure 5 plots the Overall average of each model against the speed at which it generates text for a single user. Speed is measured in characters per second, so that models with tokenizers of different densities can be compared on equal footing. Lara Mini base lies on the Pareto frontier: the seven faster models score at most 42.6, and every model that scores higher generates text at least 1.8 times more slowly. The closest of them in Overall average, MiniCPM5-2B, is 0.5 points higher but 8.7 points lower on the multilingual average. The speed advantage of Lara Mini base is largest for a single user and on long prompts, and narrows when many users share the GPU (Appendix E).

5.4  English

Table 7 reports every benchmark for Lara Mini base, the best models of its group and the best model of each larger group, and Table 19 lists the English benchmarks for all models. Its English average (66.4) is the second best of its group, 2.0 points below Trinity-Nano (68.4). Its English average lies between those of the 3B dense models SmolLM3-3B (64.7) and Ministral-3-3B (67.7).

5.5  Multilingual

Table 7 reports the multilingual benchmarks on the languages supported by Lara Mini base, and Table 20 lists them for all models. Lara Mini base ranks first in its group on seven of the nine benchmarks, and on XCOPA is tied with Gemma-4-E2B. Its lead is largest on INCLUDE (58.7, 5.3 points above granite-4.0-h-tiny). It ranks lower on the other two benchmarks, Belebele and PAWS-X. On Belebele, Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3-1.7B score up to 2.6 points higher. On PAWS-X, a paraphrase task in six high-resource languages, Lara Mini base is 1.6 points behind the best models of its group, Hunyuan-1.8B and Trinity-Nano. On T-HellaSwag, Lara Mini base is first in its group on its supported languages (58.4), and only three of the 56 models, all with more active parameters, score higher. Averaged over all the languages of the benchmarks, including those it does not support, Lara Mini base still ranks first in its group, at 49.4 (Table 21). The second, Gemma-4-E2B (49.0), supports more than 140 languages (Gemma Team, 2026), against the 45 of Lara Mini base.

5.6  Math and Code

Table 7 also reports math and code. Lara Mini base has the best math average in its group, 4.7 points above Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep. Its math average is also higher than that of every model with more active parameters except MiniCPM5-2B and five Qwen and Hunyuan models with 4B to 8B active parameters. Its code average ranks fifth in its group.

5.7  Long-Context Results

We evaluate Lara Mini base after the long-context stage (Section 4.1) at 32k and 128k tokens on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) (13 synthetic English tasks), ONERULER (Kim et al., 2025) (retrieval tasks in 26 languages) and HELMET (Yen et al., 2025) (mostly application-centric English tasks). Since Lara Mini base is a base model, it continues generating text after its answer. We therefore keep only the tasks whose scores do not depend on that text: four retrieval tasks for ONERULER and four categories for HELMET (Section D.3).

Before the long-context stage, Lara Mini base scores at most 15.0 on the three benchmarks at 32k and 128k tokens (Table 8). After it, Lara Mini base leads the five open models of Table 8 on ONERULER, the only multilingual benchmark of the three, at 32k tokens (90.1), and is second at 128k, 3.8 points behind Gemma-4-E2B. On RULER and HELMET, it trails only Qwen3.5-2B and Gemma-4-E2B, which have about three times its active parameters. The long-context stage barely changes short-context scores: on the benchmarks in Table 6, the Overall average changes by less than 0.1 points, and no domain average by more than 0.8 points.

6  Multilingual Data and Model Capacity

The introduction raised a common concern about multilingual pretraining: at small scales, languages compete for the model’s capacity (Conneau et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024). If they did in Lara Mini base, two signs should be visible. First, its multilingual data would cost English: replacing them with English would clearly raise English scores. Second, its mixture of experts would serve the languages by dividing its experts among them, so that each language uses only part of the model.

Development suite.

We scored the anneals of Section 6.1 and the short runs of Sections C.1 and C.2 on a development suite. Its 17 benchmarks are the English and multilingual benchmarks in Table 17, excluding ARC-Challenge and MMLU-Pro. MMLU-Pro remained at chance level (10%) in the short runs trained from scratch, and we exclude it from all development scores so that they all average to the same benchmarks. The development suite uses its own prompts and, unless otherwise stated, averages across all languages within each benchmark, so its scores are not comparable to those in Section 5.

6.1  Multilingual Share

To test the first sign, we branched two anneals of 100B tokens from the training run of Lara Mini base at the end of its transition stage (5.4T tokens). Both decayed the learning rate to zero and differed only in their mixture. The first used the anneal mixture of Lara Mini base, with 27% English, 33% multilingual and 40% code, math and SFT-like data. The second replaced all multilingual data with English, at 60% English and the same 40% of code, math and SFT-like data. We scored both on the development suite, averaging the multilingual benchmarks over the supported languages as in Section 5 (Figure 6).

With more than twice as much English data in the anneal, the English average rose by only 0.3 points, about a tenth of the 2.7 points that the multilingual average lost on the supported languages (Figure 6). Without multilingual data, the score was lower on eight of the nine multilingual benchmarks, by up to 4.6 points on commonsense and knowledge benchmarks such as Global PIQA, XCOPA, T-HellaSwag and INCLUDE. The multilingual data cost math and code less than half a point. On the math and code benchmarks of Section 5, the anneal with multilingual data scored 53.8 and 43.6, and the one without it 54.2 and 43.7. A likely reason for the small English gain is that, by the end of the transition stage, the model had already read more than 2T English tokens, so that additional English in the anneal added little. The test covers only the anneal: it does not measure the effect of the multilingual share during the main stage.

6.2  Expert Routing across Languages

To test the second sign, we ran the released Lara Mini base on the Belebele passages (Bandarkar et al., 2024), the same text in each supported language, and recorded the experts to which each token was routed. In each layer, we measured the Jensen–Shannon divergence between each language’s distribution over the routed experts and the mean distribution across all 43 languages (Figure 7).

Routing differs between languages in the first and last layers and is almost identical in the middle of the network, with an average divergence of at most 0.015 bits in layers 10 to 17. In layers 2 to 7, 31 of the 37 languages with a relative among the 43 route most like that relative, for example, Catalan like Spanish, Czech like Slovak, and Estonian like Finnish. The grouping follows the language rather than the script: Serbian, written in Cyrillic, routes most like Croatian, and Maltese, written in Latin script, most like Arabic. Languages, therefore, share experts rather than divide them, which is consistent with the small cost of multilingual data for English (Section 6.1). Together, the two analyses find little of the competition that the concern predicts, but they do not show whether the mixture of experts or the data selection is responsible.

These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that multilingual learning benefits from shared representations rather than requiring separate capacity for each language. This resembles the positive transfer observed in multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997) and multilingual neural machine translation (Firat et al., 2016). One possible explanation is that different languages provide complementary constraints on representations of underlying concepts, allowing the model to generalize across linguistic boundaries. However, shared expert routing does not directly establish shared semantic representations, and our experiments do not demonstrate that multilingual training improves general reasoning or English performance.

7  Conclusion

We presented Lara Mini base, a mixture of experts base model with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. It was pretrained on 6T tokens, only 41% of which were in English, and in the anneal, text from the 44 other languages is the largest domain in the mixture. Its context was then extended to 128k tokens. Among the 36 open base models with up to 2B active parameters, Lara Mini base ranks first on the Overall average, on math and on the multilingual average in the languages it supports, and second on English. It achieves this at a small inference cost: for a single user, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than every model with a higher Overall average. It is also the first among the models we compared on the multilingual long-context benchmark, ONERULER, at 32k tokens (Section 5.7). The concern that languages compete for the capacity of a small model found little support in Lara Mini base. Replacing its multilingual data with English in the anneal raised the English average by only 0.3 points and lowered the multilingual average by 2.7 (Section 6.1). Its languages also share the same experts rather than dividing them (Section 6.2).

Beyond the absence of a substantial capacity penalty, our results motivate a broader hypothesis: linguistic diversity may contribute to general-purpose intelligence by exposing a model to complementary descriptions of the world. This interpretation connects multilingual pretraining to established ideas in multi-task learning and representation learning. Testing whether language diversity directly improves general reasoning remains an important direction for future research.

Release.

We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license, and will release T-HellaSwag (Appendix F). The data pipeline and the training pool remain internal, but Sections 2 and A describe the mixture in full.

Limitations.

Lara Mini base is a base model: it is not tuned to follow instructions or for safety, and should not be deployed as an assistant without further training. Its quality varies across languages. Among the languages it supports, it scores lowest in some with limited training data, such as Azerbaijani and Bengali (Section D.2). Our analyses show that the multilingual data cost English little in the anneal. They do not measure the effect of these data during the main stage, nor show which of our choices keeps the cost small.

Future work.

We plan to post-train Lara Mini base into an instruction-following model, extend the training to larger budgets and more languages, and further study how the multilingual share of the mixture affects each language and English. We also plan controlled experiments that vary linguistic diversity during the main pretraining stage, while keeping compute, total tokens, and data quality comparable, and measure the effects on English, math, code, and multilingual performance.

Appendix

Appendix A details the data mixture: the sources and licenses for each data group, the tokens in each group in the pool and at each stage, and the share of each language. Appendix B completes the training recipe with the optimizer, the choice of learning rate, the stability of the run, its parallelism, and the settings for the long-context stage. Appendix C reports the small-scale ablations behind the architecture and the optimizer. Appendix D gives the evaluation protocol, the results of all 56 models on every benchmark, the results of Lara Mini base in each language and the protocol of the long-context evaluation. Appendix E describes how we measured inference speed and reports it for Lara Mini base and 45 of the compared models. Appendix F describes T-HellaSwag, the translated benchmark we will release, and Appendix G gives the model card.

Appendix A Data Mixture in Detail

Within each domain, the training pool is divided into data groups by kind of data and by quality.

A.1  Personal and Harmful Content

We do not add our own filters for personal information or harmful content and rely on each source’s processing. Common Crawl, the origin of most of our web data, respects robots.txt at crawl time. FineWeb-2, FineWeb2-HQ, and FinePDFs anonymize email and IP addresses; HPLT 3.0 filters adult content and credentials; and FineWeb-Edu filters adult content. Some personal information and harmful content remain in the training data, as in any web-scale corpus.

Appendix B Training

B.1  Training Details

Optimizer.

Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) replaces the update of a weight matrix with an orthogonalized version of its momentum, computed with five Newton–Schulz iterations. We use Nesterov momentum with coefficient 0.95. Muon updates every two-dimensional weight inside the layers: the attention projections, the input and output projections of the Gated DeltaNet layers, and the routed and shared experts. Queries, keys and values are orthogonalized separately, and so is each expert. AdamW handles the tied embedding, the normalization weights, the routers, and the one-dimensional and convolutional parameters of the Gated DeltaNet layers. Following Liu et al. (2025), we scale each orthogonalized update by 0.2​max⁡(nin,nout)0.2\sqrt{\max(n_{\mathrm{in}},n_{\mathrm{out}})}, which matches its root-mean-square size to that of an AdamW update. All parameters therefore share a single learning rate and a decoupled weight decay of 0.1.

Learning rate.

The ablations in Appendix C used a learning rate of 1.2×10−31.2\times 10^{-3}, but the 6T run has twice their batch size and 60 times their number of tokens, so we tuned it again. Since a sweep over 6T tokens was out of reach, we measured how the optimal learning rate varies with training length and extrapolated the trend to 6T. The sweep ran on a quarter-width proxy with μ\muP (Yang et al., 2021), so that its best learning rate carries over to the full width, at the batch size of the final run and up to 74B tokens. At constant learning rate, the best value at a given length is hard to read, because the loss does not include the gain of the final decay. Reading it from averages of recent checkpoints, the best learning rate decreased with training length and extrapolated to about 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}; this estimate is biased low, since the average recovers less of the decay gain of high learning rates as training gets longer. Reading it after real decays at 22, 50 and 74B tokens, the best learning rate did not fall, which gives about 2.4×10−32.4\times 10^{-3}; this estimate is biased high, since the optimum may still fall beyond 74B. We chose 8×10−48\times 10^{-4}, close to the geometric mean of the two estimates.

Stability.

Figure 10 shows the training curves. The rare spikes of the gradient norm lasted a single step and did not move the loss. The fixed held-out set in Section 4.2 has 134M tokens, drawn as with the main-stage data. Its loss fell from 1.85 at 0.2T tokens to 1.75 at the end of the main stage, stayed there through the transition and fell to 1.63 after the anneal. The gradient norm grew slowly at constant learning rate and fell with it during the anneal. The load-balancing loss, which is 1 when all experts receive the same number of tokens, settled near 1.03 within the first trillion tokens and fell to 1.02 during the anneal.

Parallelism.

We used data parallelism and expert parallelism of degree 4, and no tensor, pipeline, or context parallelism.

Long-context stage.

Table 12 gives the settings and the data mixture of the two steps of the long-context stage (Sections 4.1 and 2.3). The part of the mixture reweighted toward long documents applies the length weights of Kolibri (Aleph Alpha, 2026) to the anneal mixture.

B.2  Software

We trained Lara Mini base with our internal training code, built on Megatron-Bridge 0.5.0 and Megatron-Core 0.18.0 (Shoeybi et al., 2019). The evaluation runs on lm-evaluation-harness and vLLM (Appendix D), and the inference benchmark on vLLM 0.28.0 (Appendix E). The released model runs in Hugging Face Transformers (Wolf et al., 2020), with the Gated DeltaNet kernels of flash-linear-attention (Yang and Zhang, 2024) when they are installed.

Appendix C Design Ablations

The main text states the result of each ablation where it describes the corresponding choice (Sections 3 and 4.1). The ablation runs were scored on the development suite defined in Section 6.

C.1  Model Class, Shape and Optimizer

We compared candidate architectures at about 0.5B active parameters (Table 13) under a protocol fixed before the first run. Each candidate was trained once on 100B tokens using the same data in the same order, with 4,096-token sequences and 1,024-sequence batches. The learning rate peaked at 1.2×10−31.2\times 10^{-3}, stayed constant up to 80B tokens and decayed to zero over the last 20B (Hägele et al., 2024). We report the mean scores on the development suite and the final model’s loss on a fixed held-out set of 128M tokens, evaluated using the same batches for every model. This loss is not comparable with the held-out loss of Appendix B. Losses at intermediate token counts are those of the average of eight constant-learning-rate checkpoints, which approximates a model annealed at that point (Li et al., 2025). These runs used global attention in every layer, and AdamW except in the last comparison. The hybrid layers (Section C.2) were adopted afterward.

Mixture of experts and shape.

The MoE was ahead of both dense models from the start. With 64 experts, the MoE ended with a lower loss than the 1.24B dense model, which has 2.4 times as many active parameters. The gap between the MoE and the 0.6B dense model was already 0.219 nats at 5B tokens and did not shrink. Doubling the experts at the same active compute reduced the loss further as training progressed, from 0.011 at 5B tokens to 0.041 at 100 B tokens. The deeper, narrower shape with 34 layers started behind (0.036 higher loss at 5B tokens) and tied the 24-layer shape at 100B. We chose it because it scored at or above the 24-layer shape on 13 of the 17 benchmarks and has 0.35B fewer total parameters. A shared expert (Dai et al., 2024), which every token passes through, adds 0.05B active parameters. The loss reduction it brought was stable from about 25B tokens on, and the model with it scored higher than the one without on 12 of the 17 benchmarks.

Muon over AdamW.

Muon (Section 4.1) used the same peak learning rate as AdamW, selected by a sweep on a half-width proxy with μ\muP (Yang et al., 2021) and confirmed at full size. With Muon, the held-out loss was lower at every intermediate point, by 0.19 at 5B tokens and by 0.04 to 0.05 from 40B tokens on. AdamW needed 1.5 times as many tokens to reach Muon’s training loss between 10B and 30B tokens, and about 1.9 times as many at 80B. Muon was also ahead on 15 of the 17 benchmarks.

C.2  Hybrid Attention

We tested how much of the global attention can be replaced by Gated DeltaNet and sliding-window attention without losing quality. Starting from the 34-layer shape with one shared expert, trained with Muon (Section C.1), we compared three variants under the protocol of Section C.1 (Table 14). The first uses Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025c) in 26 of the 34 layers, and the second uses sliding windows of 512 tokens in the same 26 layers. The third is the hybrid of Lara Mini base, with 14 Gated DeltaNet and 13 sliding-window layers arranged exactly as in Section 3.1. The remaining layers keep global attention.

Gated DeltaNet improves quality; sliding windows alone do not.

Gated DeltaNet lowered the held-out loss by a margin that appeared early in training and held to the end (Table 14). This is consistent with the lower loss of Gated DeltaNet hybrids at matched budgets reported by Merrill et al. (2026). Sliding windows alone ended up on a level playing field with full attention.

The two mixers are complementary.

On benchmarks, the two single-mixer variants were strong on different tasks (Table 15). Gated DeltaNet was better on text completion and commonsense reasoning; sliding windows were better on tasks that compare two sentences, such as entailment. The difference did not come from the length of the context, since most benchmark prompts fit within the window.

The hybrid matches the best of both.

The hybrid kept most of the loss gain of Gated DeltaNet with about half as many Gated DeltaNet layers. On benchmarks, it kept the advantage of Gated DeltaNet on completion and commonsense reasoning and recovered most of the advantage of sliding windows on entailment (Table 15). It scored above full attention on 16 of the 17 benchmarks. Its mean gain over full attention matched that of the oracle in Table 14, which neither single-mixer variant reached.

Long context.

To test whether the ranking holds beyond the training length, we extended the three variants from their 100B checkpoints with the same long-context stage. This stage trained each variant on the same 10B tokens, in 32k-token sequences, with attention masked across documents. We then evaluated them on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), its multilingual counterpart ONERULER (Kim et al., 2025) and HELMET (Yen et al., 2025) at 16k and 32k tokens, and on the 17 short benchmarks (Table 16). The hybrid was the best on RULER and ONERULER at both lengths. On HELMET, which also covers retrieval-augmented generation, re-ranking and in-context learning, the hybrid and Gated DeltaNet were level at 32k tokens and ahead of sliding windows. The hybrid led on the two categories that require reading many passages, retrieval-augmented generation and re-ranking. The extension did not hurt short-context quality: every variant gained slightly on the short benchmarks, and the hybrid remained the best.

Appendix D Evaluation Details

We run every benchmark with lm-evaluation-harness (Biderman et al., 2024) (development version 0.4.14.dev0), using its task configurations unchanged except for the number of shots, which we fix as in Table 17. Generative tasks run on vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) in bfloat16 with greedy decoding and a context of 4,096 tokens.

Baselines.

The 56 base models we compare with come from these releases: Llama 3, 3.1 and 3.2 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen2.5 (Qwen Team, 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025a) and Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026), Gemma (Gemma Team, 2024), Gemma 3 (Gemma Team, 2025) and Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), Mistral-7B (Jiang et al., 2023) and Ministral 3 (Liu et al., 2026), SmolLM2 (Ben Allal et al., 2025) and SmolLM3 (Hugging Face, 2025c), OLMoE (Muennighoff et al., 2025b), Falcon-H1 (Falcon-LLM Team, 2025), Nemotron-Flash (Fu et al., 2025), Granite 3 (IBM Granite Team, 2024), Granite 4.0 (IBM, 2025a) and Granite 4.0 Nano (IBM, 2025b), Granite 4.1 (IBM Granite Team, 2026a) and granite-swash (IBM Granite Team, 2026b), LFM2 and LFM2.5 (Amini et al., 2025; Liquid AI, 2026a; Liquid AI, 2026b) and LFM3 (Liquid AI, 2026c), Trinity (Singh et al., 2026), Hunyuan (Tencent Hunyuan, 2025), MiniCPM5 (OpenBMB, 2026), Kanana-2 (Kanana LLM Team, 2026), Tiny Aya (Salamanca et al., 2026), Apertus (Hernández-Cano et al., 2026), EuroLLM (Martins et al., 2025b), EuroMoE (Alves et al., 2026), Teuken (Ali et al., 2025), Salamandra (Gonzalez-Agirre et al., 2025), Helium (Kyutai, 2025), Luciole (OpenLLM-France, 2026), Bielik v3 (Ociepa et al., 2025), Domyn-Edge (Domyn, 2026), Limite (Prignano et al., 2026), Villanova2 (Villanova.ai, 2026) and moe-7b-1b (IBM Research, 2025).

Answer extraction.

The harness’s default extraction sometimes scores the answer format rather than the answer, so for three benchmarks we use a stricter or more complete parser, the same for every model:

  • •

    GSM8K: the first answer marked as #### N; if there is none, the first \boxed{N}; if there is none, the first “the answer is N”. We never fall back to the last number in the output.

  • •

    MGSM: the answer phrase of each language’s native chain-of-thought prompt, allowing an optional currency sign and spaces as thousands separators. The harness’s Bengali pattern is the English one, so it scores every model at zero.

  • •

    MBPP+: the MBPP generations, which must pass both MBPP’s own tests and the additional EvalPlus tests (Liu et al., 2023).

MATH uses the Minerva prompts and is scored with Math-Verify over its seven subjects (5,000 problems). CRUXEval-I and CRUXEval-O use direct prediction and the official answer parser.

D.1  Full Results

Table 18 gives the domain averages of every model we evaluated, and Tables 19, 20, 21 and 22 give every benchmark. Models are grouped by active parameters as in Table 6, larger models first, and sorted by Overall average within each group.

D.2  Per-Language Results

Figure 11 plots the score of Lara Mini base in each supported language against its training tokens in that language. Each point is the score in the language minus the benchmark mean across the non-English-supported languages, averaged over multilingual benchmarks that cover the language. Subtracting the benchmark mean removes the differences in chance level and difficulty between benchmarks. The median score of the languages Lara Mini base does not support is 20 points below that of its supported languages. Among the supported languages, the score grows only moderately with the number of training tokens (Spearman correlation 0.4). Of the three classes of language in the figure, the official EU languages, which the language weights favor (Section 2.3), have the highest median. Serbian, with 8B training tokens, scores close to Russian, which has 21 times as many. The weakest supported languages are Azerbaijani and Bengali, followed by Irish and Maltese, the two languages with the fewest training tokens.

Table 23 gives the score of Lara Mini base on every multilingual benchmark in each supported language. For each language, it compares the mean of Lara Mini base with the best mean over the same benchmarks among the 35 other models with up to 2B active parameters. Lara Mini base is ahead in 41 of the 44 languages. It trails in Simplified Chinese (Qwen3-1.7B, 2.7 points) and Bosnian (Gemma-4-E2B, 1.3 points), and is level with kanana-2-1.3b in Korean.

D.3  Long-Context Evaluation

Some tasks of RULER, ONERULER and HELMET assume a model that answers and then stops, while a base model keeps writing after its answer. Table 24 lists what we changed and why. Every model in Table 8 is scored with the same prompts, samples and code. Among them, granite-4.0-h-tiny scores low on RULER and ONERULER because it copies only two to five digits of each 7-digit number it has to retrieve.

D.4  Benchmark Contamination

Here we test whether contamination inflates the scores of Lara Mini base. HumanEval is excluded from the suite because nearly all of its items, including solutions, appear in public datasets in our pool (Section 2.2). Every other benchmark is used as released, with all its items. On MMLU and MBPP, two tests verify that items from the training pool do not inflate model’s score, against three references from its group: Llama-3.2-1B, granite-4.0-h-tiny, and Qwen3-1.7B. We divide benchmark items into clean and potentially contaminated subsets based on whether our scan identifies overlap with the training pool. This partition is applied consistently to all four models, although the training data of the reference models may differ from ours. Neither test shows signs of memorization: model’s scores are consistent with generalization.

Accuracy.

A model that had memorized the contaminated items would score higher on them than on the clean ones, relative to the references (Table 25). Lara Mini base does not: its difference is −0.2-0.2 points on MMLU (references: −0.7-0.7 to +2.0+2.0) and −9.2-9.2 on MBPP (−15.6-15.6 to −8.4-8.4). Both differences fall within the reference-model ranges, providing no clear evidence of an unusual accuracy advantage on potentially contaminated items.

Likelihood.

Memorization can also make the reference text more predictable without changing the answer. This shows in the bits per byte (BPB) of the reference text given the prompt: the reference code for MBPP, the question and its correct answer for MMLU. BPB varies across models, so only the ratio of contaminated to clean items is comparable; it is below 1 even for a model that has never seen the items, because the two groups differ in length and style. The ratio of Lara Mini base lies within the reference ranges on both benchmarks (Table 26): 0.982 on MMLU (0.940 to 0.990) and 0.763 on MBPP (0.749 to 0.806). Thus, Lara Mini base does not exhibit an unusually large likelihood advantage on potentially contaminated items relative to the reference models.

Appendix E Inference Benchmark

We measured the inference speed of Lara Mini base and of 45 of the 56 baselines of Section 5. The other 11 were not measured: 10 are not natively supported by vLLM 0.28.0 or fail to load in vLLM 0.28.0, and Villanova2-2B was added to the comparison after the benchmark. Table 27 reports the results, and Figure 5 plots the Overall average against the speed for one user.

Setup.

Each model runs on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with vLLM 0.28.0 (Kwon et al., 2023) in bf16. All models use the same engine settings, with CUDA graphs captured for batches of up to 2,048 tokens. Prompts are real text from our held-out set, cut to the exact lengths specified by each model’s tokenizer. Every number is the median of up to three repeats. Since tokenizers differ in density, from 245 to 495 tokens per 1,000 characters (273 for Lara Mini base), we report characters per second.

Appendix F T-HellaSwag: Construction and Release

T-HellaSwag is a higher-quality machine translation of HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019) into 110 language variants, which we will release. The HellaSwag test-split labels are not public, so we translated the 10,042 documents in its validation split into each variant using Lara33 3 https://laratranslate.com, Translated’s machine translation service. T-HellaSwag contains 200 of these documents per language variant, selected for translation quality and stratified by source and difficulty. T-HellaSwag-full contains all 10,042 translated validation documents per variant, without selection.

Languages.

Table 28 lists the 110 language variants: 48 for the 44 non-English languages supported by Lara Mini base and 62 for other languages. French, Portuguese and Spanish each have two regional variants, while Serbian has two script variants. The 105 languages belong to 15 families (Figure 12).

Translation.

HellaSwag draws its documents from ActivityNet Captions (Krishna et al., 2017) and wikiHow44 4 https://www.wikihow.com. Each document contains an activity label, a context and four candidate endings. The task is to choose the ending that best continues the context (Figure 13(a)). The translated document must retain one context shared by all four endings, and each translated ending must remain consistent with that context. We translated each document in four requests, one per ending. Each request sent the activity label, context and ending as separate segments (Figure 13(b)). The first request translated all three segments; requests 2 to 4 resent the translated activity label and context as non-translatable segments. For ActivityNet documents, HellaSwag splits a sentence into context and endings: the context ends with the subject, most often a short phrase such as “he” or “the man”. A subject cut off from its verb often cannot be translated correctly because, in many languages, the verb determines its case or position, or allows it to be dropped. We therefore moved this subject fragment to the start of each ending before translation. To keep activity labels consistent across documents, we also maintained a lexicon of them for each language. Each label was translated once, and subsequent requests sent its translation as a non-translatable segment. After translation, we restored wikiHow markup, such as [title], using a rule-based script in the fields where Lara had translated. We used Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026) to correct four types of translation error: fields in the wrong language or script; characters or words of another script within a field; English text left untranslated within a field; and two endings in the same document with identical translations.

Selection.

For each language variant, we selected the 200 documents with the highest translation-quality scores, stratifying the selection by source and by the difficulty of the English originals (Figure 14). We evaluated eight reference-free quality estimation (QE) models in each language variant to assess how reliably they ranked translations: CometKiwi-22 (Rei et al., 2022), CometKiwi-XL and CometKiwi-XXL (Rei et al., 2023), xCOMET-XL and xCOMET-XXL (Guerreiro et al., 2024), MetricX-24-Hybrid-XXL (Juraska et al., 2024), BLASER 2.0-QE (Dale and Costa-jussà, 2024), and COMET-poly (Züfle et al., 2025). We tested each model on 1,000 sampled documents per language variant with four corruptions of an ending: word deletion, word shuffling, replacement with another ending of the same document and replacement with an ending of another document. A model passed for a language if, for each corruption, it scored the original ending above the corrupted one in at least 95% of the comparisons. Six of the eight models passed in at least one language. In the three languages where no model passed, we used MetricX-24 alone with lower thresholds: 90% for Luxembourgish and Luganda, and 85% for West Central Oromo. The models that passed for a language scored all four endings of every document. Because a single faulty ending invalidates a document, each model rated a document by the percentile rank of its worst ending, and a document’s score was the mean of these ranks over the models that passed.

Before selection, automatic checks excluded documents containing untranslated English, fields in the wrong script or language (Kargaran et al., 2023), or retranslated fields. Selecting by translation quality alone under-represented ActivityNet: its share of the selected documents fell from 32.4% to 15.0% on average. Such a selection would therefore distort both the source and the difficulty distributions of the dataset. We divided the remaining documents into 13 strata by source (ActivityNet or wikiHow) and by the difficulty of the English original, estimated with 50 public base models. We selected the same proportion of the highest-scoring documents from each stratum, yielding 200 documents per language variant. To verify that the difficulty was preserved, we evaluated 35 additional public base models, not used to build the strata, on the selected documents. The mean absolute difference in English accuracy between the selected documents and the original split was 1.6 points, against 3.2 points when selecting by quality alone and 1.5 points for random documents from the same strata. Each language variant has its own selection of documents, so part of a score difference between two variants comes from the documents. T-HellaSwag is built to compare models within each variant.

Quality.

Automatic checks verified that every translated document was complete and that the four endings of each document shared the same translated activity label and context. On the final data, every check passed in both sets and in all 110 language variants. We compared T-HellaSwag with Multilingual HellaSwag (Lai et al., 2023). The latter’s construction differs from ours in two ways. It keeps the activity labels in English, so that each of its prompts begins with English text. It also translates the subject that ends each ActivityNet context separately from the endings, so that the two parts of the split sentence may not agree. For each of the 32 languages in both datasets, we drew 50 random T-HellaSwag documents that Multilingual HellaSwag also translates, and compared the two translations of each document. Two LLM judges, Gemini 4 Argon (Google DeepMind, 2026) and Claude Opus 5.5, preferred our translation for 98.6% and 98.7% of the documents, respectively. A human linguist reviewed 50 documents in each of Italian, French and Russian. Of the 150 documents, 145 were rated OK, 5 as having a minor error and none as having a major error.

Limitations.

Apart from the linguist review in three languages, the evidence of translation quality comes from QE models and LLM judges. No human translator revised either set, so both can contain machine-translation errors, such as stray characters and line breaks. T-HellaSwag-full is not filtered: it also keeps the documents that the automatic checks excluded from T-HellaSwag. Both sets retain the situations described in the English source, so they measure commonsense reasoning in each language variant, not knowledge specific to its culture. Because HellaSwag is public, a model that encountered an English document during training may recognize its translation.

Release.

Both sets will be released with one configuration per set and language variant, e.g., it-IT and it-IT-full for Italian. They share 50 few-shot documents per language variant from the HellaSwag training split, so that no validation document serves as a few-shot example. We translated the few-shot documents in the same way as the validation documents and selected them based on the scores from the same QE models. We score each language variant in the same way as the standard HellaSwag task scores English. The release will credit HellaSwag, wikiHow and ActivityNet Captions (Krishna et al., 2017) as sources.
